content: Do you have any other things topics that I might contribute to?

Hmm, I was thinking about asking you the same question. One adjacent topic I had in mind is term rewriting systems, which has some prior work in Rocq to reference as well. I think it really depends on your interests though, did you have anything in mind yourself?

Could you briefly list some other things happing in cslib at the moment?

I do understand a bit of other term rewriting stuff except lambda calculi, but It is not something I have invested as much time in as strong norm proofs for typed lambda calculi.

I guess I could do the term rewriting stuff though, but maybe there is something more suitable for me.

I also feel pretty comfortable with category theory upto kan extension/higher categories/infinity categories, so If you could use that, I could do it as well.
Btw, does cslib just mean "theoretical computer science library"? or do you plan on implementing other cs stuff as well?

What i'd really like to do would be a clean machine learning framework. Stuff like pytorch is very messy and incorperates a lot of runtime checks for stuff that could be done much more elegantly at compile time.

There is also a much nicer way of implementing autograd engines using total derivatives and the ideas from category theory, for instance: https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.10455

I could write a small library based on this paper. I think it is feasable to train simple classifiers that way, the goal here would not be to sell this to actual ML researchers, but have something that works but is just written down in a clean mathematical style.

But I do not know if you are interested in that, if cslib is intended to be a theoretical cs library then of course it wouldn't be appropriate.

I also feel pretty comfortable with category theory upto kan extension/higher categories/infinity categories, so If you could use that, I could do it as well.

Well, I actually got involved with CSLib initially because of interest in formalizing categorical semantics of lambda calculi. If you're interested in this, I would love to have some help.

Btw when it comes to ML theory,

  1. I think defining the VC dimension of a Boolean concept class (I.e. set system) and proving the sauer shaleh lemma would be a good start.
  2. This can be followed by a definition of various PAC learning models. I’d start with agnostic pac learning and add conditions to get noisy PAC model and simple PAC model.
  3. Alternatively you can follow the shai Ben David and shai shalev Schwartz approach.

You will need a model of queries to express various PAC models in a single framework. These PAC models rely on a sampling oracle which satisfies various conditions. I have a solution in mind for this relying on existing work…
VC dimension and Sauer Shelah are in mathlib thanks to @Yaël Dillies

I've deviated a bit from TRAAT at this point, I'm afraid, though I do have a formalization of the Birkhoff completeness theorem now. I did make the principed choice to have terms be "applicative" and signatures to be "open", though the latter choice is probably easily undone.

What model theoretic stuff did you have in mind @Chris Henson ?

I'd be interested to discuss the ARS design decisions, I'm not entirely confident I made all the right choices (though I tried to adopt the Mathlib style for notations).

For the ARS design I don't think there are any deep differences, I mainly mean reusing what core/Mathlib has defined for the various closures of relations. I also defined termination to just be an abbrev for WellFounded fun (a b : α) => r b a. Everything I've done is in the module I linked above.

For TRS I just mean that it seems that we could reuse definitions like signatures and terms from Mathlib's model theory modules. (IIRC @Bhavik Mehta suggested this idea to me, but I haven't pursued it further)

Bhavik Mehta said:

VC dimension and Sauer Shelah are in mathlib thanks to Yaël Dillies

Then I guess we can proceed to part 2. First we define a Prog that samples input output pairs. Then we define distribution dependent models for them (of course the learning algorithms can't see the distribution so they can't use it. Models are inaccessible to Progs.

  1. Agnostic PAC : Sampling (x,y) from a distribution on X×Bool\mathcal{X} \times BoolX×Bool.
  2. PAC : Take the target concept as another parameter (in addition to distribution), and return (x, f x)
  3. Noisy pac : Take noise parameter η<1\eta < 1η<1 and add noise to f x to produce (x, 1 - f x) with probability η\etaη
the query type itself as only one single query : sample, that returns an input-output pair.

Both reasonable ideas! It would definitely be a good thing to work of what is there, though I admit I don't know whether CSLib aspires to have Mathlib as a dependency.

I've found working with the Mathlib terms a bit clunky, but that's probably a result of my inexperience, or just a few missing lemmas.

Yes, we already have Mathlib as a dependency, though often we are pretty independent of it. One thing we do is extend certain Mathlib namespaces in CSLib, so you get some flexibility.

And if there's anything in this area you'd like to eventually PR to CSLib, we'd be very happy to have it!

Well let's discuss: it sounds like we have 2 concurrent formalizations of ARSes, mine does not use the standard definitions for closure and well-foundedness (though this is somewhat easy to fix, I think).

On the other hand I have some small but non-trivial facts about terms, equational logic, and rewriting but it uses "applicative" terms (terms with a single binary operation and constants) and not those from the Mathlib logic stuff. This can also be fixed but it's more effort.

I would be happy to put in the time to do this, but to be honest I'd be pretty disappointed if I did and someone else swooped in with a way more polished thing before I had time to finish.

This is definitely not my day job so I'd expect at least a couple of months to build this up.

Would this be interesting?

My motivation for ARS was a smaller scope originally: it started as just a few theorems that I needed/extracted from proofs about lambda calculi and organically evolved from there. So you might find things missing or structured in a way you find odd. Any additions or helpful tweaks are welcome. I agree with you that these are pretty easy to align.

For the rest, I do think this would be interesting! I can't know everything that's being worked on, but my impression is there's not much activity here. I don't think I've seen anything outside my own mentions of this possible line of work, which I've not pursued myself for lack of time.

Of course, Isabelle has essentially the whole corpus of the elementary theory of TRSes, and Rocq/Coq has CoLoR, but afaik no one is porting those at the moment.

I'll sleep on it, and propose something.

re trs i had a bit of a go at working through chapter 3 of term rewriting and all that: through defining terms, the syntactic rewriting and some of the semantic algebra stuff — you can see on my branch

i made the somewhat idiosyncratic decision to develop as much as possible with plane trees, ie terms without the restriction that function symbols be applied to the right number of arguments — everything on positions / substitutions / rewriting works for that, which is then lifted to terms, defined as being trees "well-formed" wrt a signature (assignment of arities to function symbols)
i didn't get all the way to birkhoff's theorem, & that's probably where the design choice would be properly tested, but i believe it's fairly complete for the syntactic side

Birkhoffs theorem needs a notion of interpretation, but the "obvious" notion on plane trees works for that. What might be harder is to then show that you can restrict to "well formed" models, i.e. models that only provide semantics for well formed terms.

For that you'd want to "lift" such models which is a little finicky: the extra terms need to be interpreted as raw syntax.

Hi, I’m interested in making a first CSLib contribution. My background is math/CS and Lean/mathlib, with experience in ML and the undergraduate CS curriculum broadly. Does anyone have any ideas on where to start, or what could be a good first contribution?

I was thinking either something in basic ML theory or something like properties or time complexity of algorithms like sorting algorithms. I'm also confused what happened to https://github.com/leanprover/cslib/pull/442 and https://github.com/leanprover/cslib/pull/446 which were closed but not merged, did mergesort/insertionsort stability get merged in another PR or something?
